items.value: Oyster
items.reasoning: A filter feeder strains suspended food particles from water. The oyster is a bivalve mollusc that pumps water across its gills and traps plankton and detritus in mucus, the textbook example of filter feeding. Catfish are bottom-foraging omnivores that pick up food items individually, the octopus is an active predator that seizes prey with its arms and beak, and the pelican scoops whole fish in its gular pouch and drains the water off rather than sieving particles.

items.value: Phosphorus cycle
items.reasoning: The phosphorus cycle is a purely sedimentary cycle with no significant gaseous phase: the natural reservoir is rock containing phosphates, and weathering releases small quantities of phosphate into the soil solution from which plants absorb it. The carbon and nitrogen cycles both have large atmospheric reservoirs (CO2 and N2 respectively) that supply the cycle, and the sulphur cycle likewise has a substantial atmospheric component from volcanic activity and biogenic gases, so in none of those three is rock weathering the main entry route.

items.value: Only earthworms, millipedes and woodlice are detritivores (1, 3 and 5 only)
items.reasoning: Detritivores feed on dead and decaying organic matter. Earthworms (1) ingest soil rich in decomposing litter, millipedes (3) consume decaying leaf litter and plant debris, and woodlice (5) are terrestrial crustaceans that feed on rotting wood and litter — all three qualify. Jellyfish (2) are carnivorous cnidarians that capture live zooplankton and small fish with stinging tentacles, and seahorses (4) are predators that suck in live copepods and small crustaceans; neither feeds on detritus. Hence 1, 3 and 5 only.

items.value: Assessing the carbon footprint of building operations around the world
items.reasoning: The Common Carbon Metric was developed under UNEP's Sustainable Buildings and Climate Initiative to provide a consistent international protocol for measuring energy use and reporting greenhouse gas emissions from the operation of buildings, so that building performance can be compared across countries. It is a building-sector measurement protocol, not an agricultural trading instrument (B), a national inventory tool (C), or a global fossil-fuel accounting method (D).

items.value: All three — cnidarians, fungi and protozoa have species forming symbiotic relationships
items.reasoning: Cnidarians (1) include reef-building corals and sea anemones, which host symbiotic zooxanthellae and shelter clownfish. Fungi (2) form two of the best-known symbioses in biology: lichens with algae or cyanobacteria, and mycorrhizae with plant roots. Protozoa (3) include the flagellates such as Trichonympha that live in the gut of termites and digest cellulose for their host. All three groups therefore contain symbiotic species.

items.value: Statements 1 and 4 only are correct
items.reasoning: The Chausath Yogini temple at Mitaoli near Morena is a circular temple attributed to the Kachchhapaghata ruler Devapala in the early fourteenth century, so 1 is correct, and its circular colonnaded plan is the basis of the widely repeated popular belief that it inspired the design of the Indian Parliament building, so 4 is correct. Statement 2 is false because other circular yogini temples exist in India, notably at Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial in Odisha and Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh. Statement 3 is false because a yogini temple belongs to the Shakta-Tantric tradition and this one houses a Shiva shrine at its centre, not a Vaishnava cult.

items.value: Dholavira
items.reasoning: Dholavira, on Khadir island in the Rann of Kutch, is celebrated for the most elaborate water management system of the Harappan world: bunds and dams were thrown across the seasonal Manhar and Mansar streams and the water was channelled into a cascading series of large rock-cut reservoirs built into the settlement itself. Kalibangan is known for its ploughed field and fire altars, Rakhigarhi for its scale and cemetery, and Ropar for being the first Harappan site excavated after Independence.

items.value: Only Broach had an English East India Company factory in the first quarter of the seventeenth century
items.reasoning: After the Surat factory of 1613 the English pushed inland and along the Gujarat coast, establishing a factory at Broach (Bharuch) alongside Ahmedabad and Agra within the following few years, so 1 falls inside the first quarter of the century. Trichinopoly (3) is an inland Tamil town that never held an early Company factory; English settlement on the Coromandel began at Masulipatnam and Armagaon and only reached Madras in 1639. Chicacole (2) in northern Andhra is not among the factories founded by 1625, so the answer is 1 only. This is the one item in this set where the negative claim about Chicacole rests on the absence of it from the early factory lists rather than on a positive date, hence the reduced confidence.

items.value: The later Guptas of Magadha, the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, the Maukharis of Kanauj and the Maitrakas of Valabhi (1, 3, 4 and 6)
items.reasoning: In the sixth and early seventh centuries northern India was divided among the later Guptas of Magadha (1), the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar (3) whose line produced Harshavardhana himself, the Maukharis of Kanauj (4) whose kingdom Harsha inherited through his sister's marriage, and the Maitrakas of Valabhi (6) in Saurashtra. The Paramaras of Malwa (2) rose only in the ninth to tenth centuries, and the Yadavas of Devagiri (5) belong to the twelfth to fourteenth centuries and to the Deccan, not to northern India, so both are ruled out.

items.value: All four — wrestling, astrology, accounting and soothsaying
items.reasoning: Fernao Nuniz's account of the Vijayanagara court describes the large body of women maintained within the palace and lists among them wrestlers, astrologers and soothsayers, and women who wrote all the accounts of the expenses incurred inside the gates as well as the affairs of the kingdom. All four listed accomplishments therefore appear in his description. Confidence is moderate only because the closely similar Portuguese account of Domingo Paes is often quoted alongside Nuniz's and the two are easily conflated.

items.value: Rabindranath Tagore translated the National Anthem from Bengali to English at Madanapalle
items.reasoning: While staying at the Besant Theosophical College at Madanapalle in 1919, Tagore rendered Jana Gana Mana into English as 'The Morning Song of India', and the anthem was set to notation there. Pingali Venkayya's flag work is associated with the coastal Andhra region around Machilipatnam and Bezwada, not Madanapalle; Pattabhi Sitaramaiah is likewise linked to coastal Andhra; and the Theosophical Society's headquarters were established at Adyar near Madras, not at Madanapalle.

items.value: Pairs 2 and 3 only — Chandraketugarh with terracotta art and Ganeshwar with copper artefacts
items.reasoning: Chandraketugarh in West Bengal is renowned for its richly modelled terracotta plaques and figurines, so pair 2 is correct, and Ganeshwar in the Sikar district of Rajasthan, close to the Khetri copper belt, has yielded a very large assemblage of copper objects, so pair 3 is correct. Burzahom in Kashmir is a Neolithic site known for its pit dwellings, bone and stone tools and a menhir, not for rock-cut shrines, so pair 1 is wrong.

items.value: Statement 1 only — Chengiz Khan reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign
items.reasoning: Chengiz Khan pursued the fugitive Khwarezmian prince Jalaluddin Mangbarni to the Indus in 1221, well within Iltutmish's reign of 1211-1236, so 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong because Timur's invasion, in which he crossed the Indus and sacked Multan and Delhi, took place in 1398 under Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah, roughly half a century after Muhammad bin Tughluq's death. Statement 3 is wrong because Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, decades after Deva Raya II, who ruled Vijayanagara until about 1446.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only are correct
items.reasoning: St. Francis Xavier was among the small group who joined Ignatius Loyola in founding the Society of Jesus in 1534, so 1 is correct, and his feast on 3 December is observed in Goa every year, with the decennial exposition of his relics, so 3 is correct. Statement 2 is false in its first half: he died in 1552 on Shangchuan (Sancian) island off the coast of China while waiting to enter the mainland, and his body was only later brought to Goa, where it rests in the Basilica of Bom Jesus.

items.value: Statement 2 only — sons claim during the father's lifetime under Mitakshara but only after his death under Dayabhaga
items.reasoning: Statement 2 states the central distinction correctly: under Mitakshara a son acquires an interest in ancestral property by birth and can therefore claim during his father's lifetime, whereas under Dayabhaga the son's right arises only on the father's death. Statement 1 is false because the two schools are regional, Dayabhaga prevailing in Bengal and Assam and Mitakshara over the rest of the country, and neither is defined by caste. Statement 3 is false as stated, since the male-only versus mixed-membership contrast is not the basis on which the two schools are distinguished, and the option set contains no combination pairing 2 with 3, which confirms that only 2 is intended to be correct.

items.value: Playwrights
items.reasoning: All three were Sanskrit dramatists. Bhavabhuti, of the eighth century, wrote Uttararamacharita, Mahaviracharita and Malatimadhava; Hastimalla was a Jain playwright whose works include Vikranta Kaurava and Maithili Kalyana; and Kshemeshvara wrote the Chandakausika. Their common identity is authorship of plays, not monastic office, temple building or philosophical exposition.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the Government of India Act, 1935 reserved seats for women in the legislature
items.reasoning: The Act of 1935 expanded the franchise and provided reserved seats for women in the provincial legislatures, so 2 is correct. Statement 1 is false: the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 did not grant universal adult franchise to women above 21; the vote remained tied to property, tax and educational qualifications, and the question of admitting women at all was left to be decided by the individual provincial legislatures, several of which enfranchised qualified women only in the years that followed.

items.value: The Quit India Resolution was adopted by the All India Congress Committee on 8 August 1942
items.reasoning: The AICC met at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay and passed the Quit India Resolution on 8 August 1942; Gandhi delivered the 'Do or Die' call the same evening and the leadership was arrested at dawn on 9 August. The Congress ministries resigned in 1939 over India's entry into the war, and the Cripps Mission with its offer of Dominion Status after the war came in March-April 1942, so options C and D belong to different dates.

items.value: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
items.reasoning: 'Songs from Prison' is the collection of English renderings of ancient Indian devotional lyrics that Gandhi made during his imprisonment at Yeravda, published in 1934 in an arrangement prepared by John S. Hoyland. Nehru's prison writings are historical and autobiographical prose rather than translations of religious lyrics, and neither Tilak's Gita Rahasya nor Sarojini Naidu's original English verse fits the description.

items.value: Paragana - Sarkar - Suba, in ascending order of size
items.reasoning: In the Mughal administrative hierarchy the empire was divided into subas, each suba into sarkars, and each sarkar into parganas, which were themselves groups of villages. Reading from the smallest upward therefore gives pargana, then sarkar, then suba, which is the order in option A; the other three options invert or scramble this hierarchy.

items.value: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
items.reasoning: Vidyasagar served as Secretary of the Hindu Female School founded in Calcutta in 1849 through the efforts of J. E. D. Bethune, and the institution was later renamed the Bethune School after its founder. Annie Besant's educational work belongs to Banaras and a later generation, Debendranath Tagore led the Brahmo Samaj rather than this school, and Sarojini Naidu belongs to the twentieth century entirely.

items.value: Officers of the Indian National Army
items.reasoning: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sehgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon were the three Indian National Army officers court-martialled together at the Red Fort in the winter of 1945-46, the trial that provoked nationwide protest and was defended by a Congress team including Bhulabhai Desai and Tej Bahadur Sapru. They belong to none of the other three contexts listed.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 — the Nizamat of Arcot emerged out of Hyderabad State and the Mysore Kingdom out of the Vijayanagara Empire
items.reasoning: The Carnatic or Arcot Nizamat was carved out of the Deccan territories administered from Hyderabad, its Nawab holding office as a deputy of the Nizam before asserting autonomy, so 1 is correct. The Wodeyars of Mysore were feudatories of Vijayanagara who established an independent kingdom after the empire's collapse following Talikota, so 2 is correct. Statement 3 is false: Rohilkhand was carved out of Mughal Katehar by Rohilla Afghan chiefs under Ali Muhammad Khan in the first half of the eighteenth century, before and independently of Ahmad Shah Durrani's invasions, so it was not formed out of territory he occupied.

items.value: Ajanta Caves lie in the gorge of the Waghora river
items.reasoning: The Ajanta caves are cut into the scarp of a horseshoe-shaped ravine of the Waghora river in the Sahyadri hills, which is exactly what option A states. The Sanchi stupa stands on a hilltop near the Betwa, not in a Chambal gorge; the Pandu-lena caves are near Nashik on the upper Godavari, not the Narmada; and the Amaravati stupa stands on the Krishna, not the Godavari.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the demand for Bangla as a national language was raised in the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is correct: Dhirendranath Datta moved in the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan in February 1948 that Bengali be recognised alongside Urdu and English, the demand that grew into the language movement commemorated on 21 February. Statement 1 is false in its attribution: International Mother Language Day was proclaimed by UNESCO, the United Nations body for education, science and culture, and not by UNICEF.
